utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody again. Mr. Milovancevic, just before you continue with your argument, may I ask a question of you that I asked of you right at the beginning of this trial and several times during the trial. And I'm asking you this question because it will help the Chamber, or at least me, to understand where you're going with your argument. Are you able to tell us in one way what the theory of the Defence case is? In other words, what's your defence? Self-defense? Alibi? Military justification? Just in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, Your Honours. Thank you for putting this question to me. I have a duty to answer it. This is not an alibi defence case. This is not a defence which generally deals with self-defense. This is a defence that deals with the nature of the conflict in the territory of a sovereign country, Yugoslavia, a UN member. It also deals with the existence of armed rebellion in that area, organised by Croatian leadership. It deals with the issue of which forces participated in the conflict and in which way, what happened in the conflict, and what are the actual facts of the events out in the field, starting in 1990 until the arrival of the UN troops and the final Croatian operations Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I just asked for a defence in one sentence. Again, what you are saying is what you have been saying in your case from the beginning right through, even in your argument yesterday. Could you just say to us my defence is self-defense. I am not saying it is self-defense. I'm just giving you an example, self-defense or alibi or.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood this, Your Honours. I apologise. I was too elaborate and not specific enough. Therefore, our defence case is that there was no joint criminal enterprise; that this was a case where regular state organs, all organisations, and individuals subordinated to regular state organs acted under the circumstances of armed rebellion. Nobody ever instigated, ordered, planned, in any way, the commission of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. You deny the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. That's your defence? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that defence cover the entire counts, or does it cover just the allegation of the JCE?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It pertains to all encounters and to each and every specific paragraph of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also every specific paragraph of pre-trial brief and final brief. Thank you. Your Honours, by your leave I would like to continue or begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed with your argument, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following this theory of defence that we just elaborated in our brief answer to the Bench, the Defence, yesterday, pointed out to the evidence led by the Prosecution, by way of which the Prosecution demonstrated that there was an armed rebellion in the territory of the sovereign Yugoslavia. This armed rebellion was confirmed by witness Imre Agotic. In a case where there is an armed rebellion in the territory of a country, or rather, this is regulated specifically by Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol II from 1977. We will revert to this question somewhat later. What Defence wishes to state now is that the Prosecution witness, Imre Agotic, when speaking of Saborsko and the situation as it existed there, directly confirmed that this was not a case of the story as it was depicted by the Prosecution here of a defenceless Croatian village where civilians were persecuted, but rather that this was a system of villages from Saborsko down to Licka Jesenica, where all residents, as Agotic said, were armed. As for the events in Saborsko in November of 1991, Colonel Agotic, as a highly placed official in the then-Tudjman government, said that the map of the attack, the one used by the Prosecution, did not come from the JNA; because had that been the case, it would have been necessary for it to have a signature of the commander and indication of his rank. Witness Agotic, the Prosecution witness, confirmed that looking at the content of the map he came to conclusion that this was the map of the 5th Partizan Brigade, which had been stationed in the Saborsko area. Prosecution witness Agotic confirmed that Partizan Brigades were established in the process of mobilisation. They were established by the JNA; that these brigades were under the command of JNA units and that they were manned by local residents, which was duty-bound to serve in such brigades for the purposes of defence. This is Exhibit 398, page 20313. Therefore, up until the 2nd of July, 1991, Agotic was a colonel of JNA, intelligence officer, and he was very well aware of how Partizan Brigades were established. He should be believed on this count. Unlike his evidence, the evidence of this Prosecution witness, or rather, contrary to his evidence, the Prosecution kept claiming yesterday that it was Milan Martic who was creating TO units, both in Saborsko and in all other places of Krajina, which is impossible under the law, under the constitution, and under the regular procedure as it existed, because in 1991 there was a regular armed force in Yugoslavia, that was the JNA. There was the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, which had certain authorities and discharged them in that area. Colonel Agotic confirmed that Tactical Group 2 was established in Belgrade; that means that it was established - at least that is my understanding of his statement - that it was established by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in Belgrade, that there was a TO in Plasko. And based on the map that we spoke of earlier, one could see that on the basis of the operation in Saborsko, there was air support from 8.40 to 9.10 hours and there was an artillery preparation and artillery support, both of which were planned in advance. All of these facts indicated that this was not just an operation of TO members, but rather, that Partizan Brigades participated in it and they were legal units of the JNA. Colonel Maksic, also Prosecution witness, confirmed that all units of TO and any other units consisting of volunteers, policemen, which participated in the operations in the field, were subordinated to the commander of the most senior JNA unit. Through witness Agotic, the Prosecution tendered a number of documents: Exhibit 413 dated 12th of October, 1991. It was signed by witness Agotic on behalf of the General Staff of the Croatian army. Exhibit 414, on the 18th of October, 1991, it was also signed by witness Agotic on behalf of the General Staff of the Croatian army. Exhibit 417, 11th of November, 1991, is an order of the General Staff or Main Staff of the Croatian army sent to the operations zones of Croatian army in Osijek and Vinkovci. It was signed by General Tus. And, finally, Exhibit 418, 20th of November, 1991, is a letter of an officer of Croatian army, Imre Agotic, to the command of the 5th Army District in Zagreb. These documents directly confirm the Defence thesis. They are an evident proof of the fact that there was an armed rebellion in which Croatian officers, including General Tus, commander of JNA air force, and Colonel Agotic, intelligence officer of the JNA, deserted the JNA. They crossed over to the rebel side of Croatian formations, and then they wrote a letter. A deserter, Agotic, wrote a letter to the command of his own 5th Military District. He was a defector. There is no greater proof of the fact that this was a case of armed rebellion. This is something that the Prosecution proved via their exhibits and witnesses. When discussing the issue of whether in the territory of SAO Krajina, or rather, these areas depicted by the Prosecution as areas where the alleged JCE was in place, when we are discussing the issue of whether the JCE was in place there with a morbid goal, criminal goal, of persecuting all non-Serb population, when discussing this it is useful to point out, Your Honours, that precisely these areas, which the Prosecution painted as the areas where the crimes were committed, were the areas under the UN protection. The evidence adduced during the trial -- rather, Security Council report 23 -- 280, which is Exhibit 104, this document discusses the general concept of the Vance Plan, the concept of Vance and Mark Goulding, who was the under-secretary of UN. They wanted the UN troops to come to those areas in Croatian where Serbs represented a majority population or a significant minority, and where interethnic tensions had caused a conflict to break out. This Exhibit, 107, is mentioned by the Prosecution in paragraph 12; namely, that the role of the UN troops was to ensure that peace prevailed in that area, that these areas remained demilitarised, and that everybody be protected from the fear of an armed attack. I guess this protection pertained to Serbs as well, to Serbs who represented the majority population in that area. What the Prosecution directly alleges is that the UN troops came to that area where previously Yugoslav authorities, with the president of Serbia and with the Serbian leadership of Serbian Krajina, had organised a joint criminal enterprise. It cannot be that the UN was that naive and that they allowed themselves to be tricked in this way. This is something that is a pure construction of the OTP, and this is further confirmed by the evidence of their expert, Ivan Gruic. We objected to him coming here to testify because he was a colonel of the warring side, Croatia. He was in their forces from the beginning to the end. He is a high official of Croatia who is included in the indictment against Markac and Cermak, an indictment for a joint criminal enterprise which ended in the expulsion of Serbs from Croatia. He is a high government official of a government which is indicted by this same Prosecution for a crime. And now they're using him to deal with the issue whether the Serbs were expelled or not. Now let us turn to something else; namely, to the issue of how ridiculous this JCE is a story and just how radically different it is from reality. This expert, Gruic, in his report stated that in the territory of the Republic of Croatia during the period covered by the indictment, 11.834 persons were killed. Therefore, 11.834 persons. He confirmed here in the courtroom that several hundred corpses had been exhumed from the areas where the Operation Storm was executed in 1995. He said that 68 corpses were uncovered as a result of the Flash Operation. Maybe the number of victims comes up to 1.000, and we have to ask ourselves where these 11.834 persons were killed during the same period in the conflict of the same warring parties; whereas, in their indictment, the Prosecution states that 354 persons were killed in this joint criminal enterprise. It was difficult for me to add up these numbers. People cannot be referred to as numbers, but I simply had to do this. Therefore, in the territory of Krajina, which constitutes one-third of the territory of Croatia, according to the Prosecution, Martic, who is a criminal, according to them, killed 354 persons; whereas, during that same period of time the Prosecution -- another 10.800 persons were killed. And this is the Prosecution is concealing from you. This is a figure used by their expert witness, Gruic. You travelled to that area. You could see that there was no Chinese wall separating Krajina from the rest of Croatia. There is no wall as the one that separates Palestinians from the rest of that territory, no 6-metre high wall. This is an open area. And we now we have to see who did what in the territory of Croatia in 1991 that resulted in the killing of so many people and exactly what kind of an enterprise it was. This is something that the Prosecution showed through their witnesses; namely, that this was an armed rebellion aimed at the destruction of Yugoslavia, defeat of the JNA, in order to create an independent Croatia. The Prosecutor really put in a lot of effort to prove how correct the statement made by Mr. Tudjman in 1992, in the main square in Zagreb in Croatia, how true his sentence was that there would have been no war had Croatia renounced its independence. Croatia needed the war to gain its independence. I don't know if my sentence was correct or not. It is our contention that he said that there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it, yet Tudjman said there would have been no war had he renounced our independence. The armed rebellion served to achieve this goal, the independence of Croatia; this was an illegal goal, an aim that was in contravention of international law, as confirmed by our expert witness Professor Smilja Avramov and all the other witnesses. This was an act in contravention of the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask a question, Mr. Milovancevic. Do I understand you to be saying that because Croatia wanted war to gain its independence and this was an act of rebellion, therefore, the rest of Yugoslavia, including Serbia and RSK, were justified in containing this rebellion by whatever means and at whatever cost? Is that what -- they had to discipline this recalcitrant member of the Yugoslav republic; is that what I understand you to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, you did not quote me completely accurately, but that would be the essence of our case. Because when it comes to the Geneva Protocol II, modern law draws a distinction between rebellion and civil war. Rebellion continues to be within the jurisdiction of the state, and the international law no longer, or rather, does not apply to it at all. In accordance with Article 1, paragraph 2 of the Geneva Protocol appended to the Geneva Conventions, this is so. All legal systems in the world qualify and have qualified as a serious crime the armed rebellion. And the use of armed force to defend the constitutional order is something that is envisaged in all the legal systems of the world. I have noted that perhaps you did not interpret my words completely accurately, because I have not said anything about the participation of Serbia or any other parties in the efforts to suppress the rebellion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The federal state, the federal authorities had the right to suppress the rebellion. If I misunderstood you, I withdraw my remark. I have to apologise for making it if I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't misunderstand me. I mentioned the federal government because -- maybe I made a mistake to say Serbia. I should have said the federal government, and the federal government because of the involvement of the JNA. Let me just ask you this one question: What is the distinction between a rebellion and a civil war? And at what stage does the transition come from the one to the next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, both rebellion and civil war are states or conditions that can co-occur, and one can follow from another. And in the territory of the whole of Yugoslavia, this is precisely what happened. International law envisages quite clear restrictions when it comes to the obligation to respect human rights when it comes to civil war, and there are specific provisions in the international law for that. These restrictions at any rate refer to or cover all armed activities by all armed forces, and they also cover the suppression of armed rebellion because the suppression of armed rebellion cannot be used as the pretext for the commission of crimes. This is something that is uncontestable. When it comes to civil war, however, I simply wanted to say something that is quite important for the Defence. The Geneva Conventions from 1949 and the Protocols I and II, in fact, Article 4 of Protocol II, these are the provisions for civil wars. And these restrictions as to the obligation to abide by the provisions of humanitarian law do not infringe the sovereignty of the state, because no article in this protocol can be invoked in order to infringe the sovereignty of a state or the right of any government to maintain or re-establish law and order within its state or to protect its territorial integrity and national unity. Paragraph 2 -- let me please finish. This is very important. Article 3, paragraph 2, states that no provision in this article can be invoked to justify a direct or indirect intervention for any reason in an armed conflict or internal or foreign affairs of a high contracting parties -- party where the conflict occurred. So the Defence cannot give you an answer to your question in one sentence, but the entirety of the closing argument will show to you the distinction and provide to you an answer. As regards the text that I just quoted about the prohibition to jeopardise the sovereignty by invoking Article 3 of Protocol II, let me just point out to you a very striking example. The Prosecution itself accepted that the president of the Yugoslav Presidency, Mr. Mesic, the man who hailed from a rebel state, an extremist that was appointed to this post under the pressure of the European Community, so he was the head of the state, and there was pressure to appoint him to that post, regardless of the fact that he was from a seceding state. This was -- this means that the sovereignty of the state was, in fact, infringed. And we saw that this man said on the 5th of December, 1991, "I performed my task; Yugoslavia is no more." And he received a frenetic applause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can I give you a word of advice. When the Bench wants to ask a question, it is advisable to give the Bench that opportunity. Because whatever you say without giving that opportunity may be very important but it just passes, because I'm worried about -- for me to understand what you are saying, I would like to ask my question at that point. And if you carry on before I ask my question and I don't understand what you are saying. Let me ask my question. At two stages you talked about a rebellion, and I asked you a question: What is a distinction between a rebellion and a civil war? You haven't answered my question. But initially when you talked about the rebellion, I got the impression that you are saying it is totally an internal issue, no international interference can come in. Later when you spoke about the rebellion, you seemed to suggest that the Geneva protocols are applicable to that kind of situation and international humanitarian law is applicable to that situation and that the international community can come in, but you also said it's applicable also to civil law -- to civil war. Now, I don't -- please, don't go into a long story. Just tell me: Is international law, according to your submissions, applicable to a rebellion, yes or no? I'm trying to get the distinction between a rebellion and a civil war. Just say yes or say no. Don't elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to the armed rebellion, and let me just say one more thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misquoted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The provisions of the Protocol II of the Geneva Conventions relating to Article 3. They do not prohibit the possibility of an intervention, they prohibit the intervention by foreign states in the affairs of a sovereign state, even when there is a civil war. And since you asked me again about the difference between an armed rebellion and civil war, perhaps I could give you a brief answer, one sentence. Civil war is a situation that occurs in the territory of a state when the authorities are unable to function, when the authorities are unable to maintain law and order and to prevent armed conflict, and when everybody is at war with everybody else. When you have religious or political or any other strife in various areas, various stages of intensity, various ways, armed rebellion is an organised activity on the part of the rebel authorities, rebel political structures, or rebel units that strive to gain an area that they want. They conduct armed activities there in order to defeat the legal authorities. That would be an answer in a nutshell to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not a nutshell. It's a very long answer. It's unlike what I've asked from you. And this is the problem and you keep complaining that I'm misquoting you. And I'm going to continue misquoting you if you can't give me succinct, clear, short, to-the-point, focused answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you keep telling me this, then I don't understand what you're talking about. If you answer my question directly, then I understand. And the reason you're getting misquoted is simply because I don't understand what you're saying. If you read what is written -- maybe you understand what you're saying when you talk in B/C/S, but you must read the English. You will begin to see that I really don't understand what you say most of the time, and I've got a difficulty asking my questions. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before proceeding, I would like to pose two questions to you, Mr. Milovancevic. First of all, I would like to know the state of armed rebellion. Is the Defence saying that it was on ongoing state of armed rebellion during the entirety of the period set forth in the indictment; or was it more than one armed rebellion? I would like that question to be answered. I don't know if you intend to deal with it later on in your submissions, but that is the first question. And the next question would be: For the purposes of the armed rebellion, you stated that the federal authorities had the right to suppress the rebellion. Now, who constituted the federal authority, having this right during the course of that indictment period? Was it a federal authority of Croatia? And please address the question as to whether it would have been the "government" of the SAO K or of the RSK, but I would like the question addressed within that sphere. Are you understanding me, Mr. Milovancevic? I don't know if you intended to deal with these points later on in your submission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your questions are quite specific, Your Honour, and let me reply. I wanted to do so at a later stage, but perhaps it would be easier for me to do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. No, if you intend to deal with it at a later stage, then I would find that quite sufficient, but I just did not know whether you intended to cover it. You need not answer the questions now; but if you're able to, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address this issue now, Your Honour. Under international law, rebellion is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the state. International law does not apply to it. This is an internal affair of the state. And the federal state of Yugoslavia, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, the federal government, the Yugoslav Presidency, and the JNA, as the regular armed force - which includes the TO - had to suppress it using all means, this rebellion in other words. The -- there was a rebellion in parts of the territory of the sovereign state of Yugoslavia in 1990 and 1991, all the way until 1992 when Yugoslavia de facto ceased to exist. This rebellion was organised by the Croatian authorities in the territory of what was then the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, and by the Slovenian authorities in what was then the Yugoslav Republic of Slovenia. This is where it all began. The rebellion was not suppressed by the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was suppressed by no one but the federal authorities in Belgrade, the Yugoslav Presidency, the federal defence ministry, the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence, the federal government, and the JNA. So that would be a brief answer to your question, and I will deal with this topic at length in the course of my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You are saying then that the RSK and the SAO K had no part whatsoever? They did not join in any way in the quashing of the rebellion, or they would have no vested interest or right in the quashing of this rebellion? That is why I put it within the sphere of Croatia, even though I acknowledge that they're not federal territories. But the persons who were allegedly committing the acts in this case are persons who are acting on behalf of the RSK and the SAO K. And, initially, certainly it would have been still under the umbrella of Croatia. Are you seeing my point? There was no joinder at any point in time between those entities then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I understand your point fully. Your Honour, yes, I understand the question that you're asking me. In the opinion of the Defence, the essence lies in the fact that the federal authorities, the federal state of Yugoslavia, the Presidency, the JNA, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, have the duty and the right in accordance with the constitution and the international law to operate on every square metre of the territory of the Yugoslav state, regardless of what federal unit it was; Slovenia, Macedonia, or any republic in between. When I spoke about the RSK, I said that the federal authorities had the exclusive jurisdiction to suppress the armed rebellion in the territory of Croatia using the federal troops, and the RSK, the SAO Krajina, the TO, the police come into all this simply by force of necessity. These are parts of Yugoslavia within what was then the rebel Republic of Croatia that were loyal to the federal state, to the federal government, and they had the duty to comply with all the orders of the federal government regarding the mobilisation, the operation of local units, the police, as were, indeed, all those -- as indeed they were obliged to comply with all the provisions of the international law. I will deal with this at length later on. I don't know if you have any questions that pertain to this topic or perhaps I could just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please move on. Thank you. I understand the submissions which you have made. I don't know if my brothers would wish to ask anything more, but for my purposes you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So far we have mentioned two pieces of evidence in which the Prosecutor proved the existence of an armed rebellion, but these are not the only two pieces of evidence we have. Prosecution witness Colonel Radislav Masic heard here in this courtroom testified that there was an armed rebellion, that what was happening on the territory of Yugoslavia amounted to armed rebellion. He explained that Croatia and Slovenia in June 1991 issued a decision on secession from Yugoslavia, that Slovenia illegally took over the border-crossings of the federal state towards Italy and Austria, that the federal government intervened in order to re-establish control without any military operations, and that on that occasion the JNA was attacked by Slovenian territorials organised by the rebel authorities of Slovenia, who killed at least 19 JNA soldiers. Prosecution witness Colonel Maksic confirmed that after this Croatia surrounded and blocked JNA barracks. Croatia did not have the right to attack the JNA, so this can be described as armed rebellion, and this is on page 1210 to 1211. Witness Theunens also confirmed this, but he evaded saying that this was armed rebellion. He works for the OTP, and he does not want to mention that international law should apply here because this goes against the Prosecution case. Colonel Maksic testified to the fact that JNA barracks had existed for many years on the territory of all the federal republics, all over the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including Croatia; that they were frequently located in urban areas. And we could see this for ourselves. We saw the Ministry of Defence in the centre of town. We saw Pleso airport which is a military airport in the town itself. We saw this in Knin where there are barracks in the very town. They were formerly JNA barracks and they are now Croatian army barracks. Witness Maksic explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have - and if so where - evidence to the effect that Pleso airport is a military airport? I know it was said that some military equipment was kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both Prosecution and Defence witnesses mentioned Pleso airport. I don't know whether we have any documents, but this is an airport with a dual purpose; military and civilian. UNPROFOR, as a military component of the UN, was based at Pleso also. Prosecution witness Maksic, referring to armed rebellion, confirmed that in June and July 1991 - and let me remind you that Croatia seceded on the 25th of June, 1991 - many Croatian soldiers and officers deserted from the JNA. That's on page 1213. He said that this referred to a large number of men. General Djukic, Defence witness, said this was 7.000 officers who had been members of the JNA, and 62 percent of these were JNA members of Croatian ethnicity. About 7.000 Croats, who were members of the JNA, deserted. We saw that Imre Agotic, a JNA colonel, and General Tus, the commander of the air force, became later on the highest ranking officers of the rebel army, the so-called Croatian army. Witness Maksic, a Prosecution witness, explained that every member of the JNA took an oath to serve honourably and to protect the sovereignty and integrity of the state of Yugoslavia. He pointed out that these deserters, ethnic Croats, were JNA officers. An officer's honour is held sacred in every country and every nation, Your Honours. These officers deserted and trampled on their oath and even went so far as to join the rebel side. Prosecution witness Maksic said that in doing so, they betrayed their country, Yugoslavia. It was not only Tus and Agotic, but also the commander, the so-called commander, of the defence of Skabrnja. Marko Miljanic, a JNA officer, commanded the Independent Skabrnja Battalion fighting against the hostile JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm very sorry to interrupt. I would never have imagined to have to do this, but I think that Defence counsel has very specifically described the protected witness in such a way that could easily identify him. And so I think it is -- I have to rise to ask that there be a redaction of that portion. It's from page 19, line 21, and I think probably as a matter of prudence it would be best to redact that whole paragraph all the way to page 20, line 5. But certainly the beginning gives very specific details and anyone would know who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am shocked, Your Honours. What matters to the Prosecutor at this stage. I said "Witness MM-80." If somebody will guess who MM-80 is, that's his problem. I didn't give any other details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have given lots of details. You have given a lot of details. And now, given that response, the Chamber will order that from page 19, line 21, to page 20, line 5, that whole paragraph be redacted. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Prosecution witness, MM-80, confirmed that at his home and at another officer's home a cross was inscribed, and he understood it as a signal that he was to be liquidated as a JNA officer and a Serb. JNA Colonel Peric testified to something similar. This Prosecution witness said that, as a security officer, he knew that the Croats were arming themselves in his area of responsibility. The HDZ was arming local communes and villages. The aim of the HDZ was the independence of Croatia; transcript page 5291. With respect to the arming of local communes, we have Exhibit 1.005, a letter written by 142 members of the Zadar SUP dated from October 1990, stating that the Croatian MUP, Tudjman's MUP, was confiscating weapons from the reserve police force and distributing them to the Croatian population in Zadar, Benkovac, and Obrovac, exclusively on an ethnic basis. And this was evidence that an armed rebellion was being prepared. This witness stated that the reason for the JNA intervention in Skabrnja were frequent incidents and activities by Croatian units. Some of their units were located in the Skabrnja area. They organised incursions on the road in the direction of Benkovac and Zemunik airport. MM-80 says they opened fire on JNA vehicles and convoys moving along the road. This Prosecution witness confirmed here in the courtroom and drew a map, which is Exhibit 784, showing that all the roads between Benkovac and Zemunik, the Zadar airport, were impassable, and that the JNA, which is the legal and regular armed force of the country of Yugoslavia, had to cross meadows and pastures in order to reach Zemunik airport. This Prosecution witness confirmed the authenticity of documents, Prosecution documents, and that's Exhibit 785, a letter by General Vukovic, the corps commander dated the 20th of November, 1991, who says that JNA barracks in Sibenik, Split, and Zadar were blocked, that attacks on Zemunik airport had been ongoing for the past four days. And we wish to point to an interesting detail. On the 20th of November, General Vukovic informed his command and the European community that attacks on Zemunik airport had been ongoing for the past four days. The action in Skabrnja took place on the 18th of September -- on the 18th. This witness stated that during the attack on Skabrnja, as well as in any other situation, JNA soldiers were not ordered to expel the civilian population or to commit any crimes against the civilian population. That's page 5303 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Prosecution witness Marko Miljanic testified that in May 1991, he left the JNA; that in September 1991, he became the commander of the Independent Skabrnja Battalion; that he had seven villages and a third of the territory of Zadar municipality under his command, which amounts to a third of the territory of a town on the soil of Yugoslavia, a sovereign state and a member of the UN. It was under the control of a JNA deserter and his illegal forces. He had weapons at his disposal. He had 242 men who were armed with light machine-guns taken from the JNA barracks in Gorski Kotor. This Prosecution witness explained that there were two roadblocks in the village towards the Serb side. There were trenches. He himself laid minefields. He explained he laid a hundred anti-personnel and ten anti-tank mines in Skabrnja. The other minefield was above Zemunik. He testified that the Crisis Staff from Zadar, which was under the authorities of Tudjman, ordered evacuation of civilians from Skabrnja on the 20th of November, 1991; and that on the 18th of November, more than 20 members arrived in Skabrnja with anti-tank weapons. Imagine any sovereign country in this world, if someone were to bring a unit of 20 men with anti-tank rockets on its soil, how the authorities of that state respond. He confirmed that in Skabrnja the units held the line until a certain point in time, 11.30, and then the line was pierced. The document of General Vukovic shows that there were 14 JNA barracks in Zadar. According to the documents tendered by the Prosecution, they were surrounded with minefields, all kinds of weapons. They were fired on. And there were agreements reached that the siege should be lifted, and then they were not complied with. On the 20th of November, 1991, Split, Zadar, Sibenik, and Zemunik airport were all blocked. With respect to Zemunik airport, we should say that this was a military airport, but also there was a military academy there, the only military academy for the training of pilots of the JNA, the federal army. It contained very expensive equipment. The use of this equipment was made impossible when all these roads were blocked, and one should bear this in mind. Luka Brkic, another Prosecution witness, also confirmed that there was an armed rebellion. He said in Skabrnja, we had east German camouflage uniforms, belts, boots. We had automatic rifles. Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunic's note, Exhibit 107, speaks of something similar. There were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down when enumerating the number of different kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters are saying could you please slow down, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would kindly ask the interpreters to always warn me not to refrain from doing that. Sometimes it's hard for me to maintain acceptable pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is you that should remember to keep an acceptable pace. Carry on, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to mortars, automatic rifles, cases with ammunition, a rocket -- hand-held rocket-launcher was also captured. As Marko Miljanic said from the barracks in Gorski Kotor, 37 hand-grenades were captured. As for the document composed by Ernest Radjan, the JNA officer, about the sanitization of the terrain, Exhibit 109, under item 12 of that the document, he mentions the barracks called Andrija Artukovic in a garage in Skabrnja, down-town Skabrnja. We tried to find it when we were there, but a new garage was built there. Before the sanitization, the JNA officer Radjan, stated, or rather, recorded the location of each victim found, whether there was civilians or soldiers, what position they were found, what was their age. Every single detail was recorded honestly and thoroughly, and his report should not be doubted. And, therefore, this man says that is in the Andrija Artukovic barracks, Skrabnja, there was a lot of equipment, radio equipment, and other equipment. So this was an armed rebellion, Your Honours. However, this is not an end to the Prosecution evidence on the existence of armed rebellion. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) He explained that in the field they stopped wearing any insignia showing that they were members of the Federal Commission, because that could have been caused problems for them, problems from Croatian paramilitary members and residents. Witness MM-79 said that they were afraid they could be harmed, that they received threats. There was some cases of excessive behaviour. This is quite telling, isn't it, that the Croatian residents had the same attitude towards UN troops. This is what General Morillon told us. When we got to Zagreb, we were supposed to take our uniforms off so that we wouldn't be threatened. This is the attitude that the population had with respect to UN troops as a result of the government propaganda. As for Croatian authorities, the leadership, let me remind you of witness Kirudja, who spoke of the racist attitude of Janko Bobetko, commander of the Main Staff, who was a European and who had respect only for UNPROFOR members from Nordic countries; that is to say, white people. What a fine man, what fine authorities. So the Prosecutor says there was no reason to be afraid; whereas, the Prosecutor himself comes from the country which is all too fully aware of racial hatred. This Prosecution witness, MM-79, said that in the beginning of these conflicts around Knin and Drnis, the Croats manned check-points and roadblocks. See, this fact was concealed from you, Your Honours. The witness explained. He said initially there was a police check-point outside of the village of Drnis; and then some 500 metres further, there would be another roadblock manned by Croat volunteers and ZNG members. So this is Croatian armed force. And then the witness goes on to say there would be a Serb roadblock manned by local Serb residents, and there was some sort of reserve policemen there in uniforms. Can you tell the difference between the position of the Serb residents on roadblocks and Croatian forces? It was that the Serb residents were loyal to the federal state. Both TO members and police were members of regular forces of the then-existing sovereign state of Yugoslavia. Therefore, their status, according to the constitution and the law, was a regular one. As for the ZNG members, those were new forces and they were loyal to Croatian authorities which organised the armed rebellion, and their status was illegal and unconstitutional. This witness testified that between Drnis and Polje, there was a main Serb check-point but not a roadblock. He said that the majority of the people wore police uniforms and that they were quite cooperative. This witness of the Prosecution said that they had attempted to ensure that local residents would not -- would not erect roadblocks, and this is something also confirmed by witness (redacted), Defence witness; or rather, we have to redact this. Witness MM-96, I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, Your Honours.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a protected witness, MM-96. It was a slip of the tongue, I apologise, Your Honours, and I fully agree with what my learned friend asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then page 27, line 12 shall be redacted. After that, we shall redact from page 22, line 15 to page 23, line 2. We'll also redact page 25, line 17 to line 20. Okay. Those three redactions, please. Thank you very much. You may proceed now, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will bear that in mind, yes. This witness, MM-79, was out in the field from mid-May until late June of 1991. And he says police forces, Serb police forces, manning the roadblocks were cooperative with respect to him, a representative of the federal government. As for the roadblocks on the Croatian side, he said that they were manned by local residents, members of the ZNG, and in some cases policemen. Members of the ZNG were especially allergic to the army, the federal army. The ZNG was a leading force; however, when the policemen were there at the roadblocks, they had the upper hand on those barricades. Page 2.139 of the transcript. And just one more sentence. ZNG members were positioned near Kijevo, page 3.150. So the operation in Kijevo was on the 26th of August, 1991. In the course of June, 1991, this was not just the case of a police station in Kijevo manned by 150 men, Your Honours, but rather that the ZNG was deployed to the positions around Kijevo. That's a very telling fact, Your Honour. I think it's time for our break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll take our break now and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, Your Honours, we mentioned the evidence of witness MM-79, witness for the Prosecution, who said that from mid-May to the 20th of June, 1991, he saw members of the ZNG at the positions around Kijevo, deployed in that area. This is -- this was fully and directly confirmed by the evidence of General Djukic, Defence witness, who said that on the 26th of June, 1991, he received an order to place a buffer zone in several areas; that the JNA under these circumstances did, in fact, place a buffer zone; that these buffer zones existed; that efforts were made in addition to this Federal Commission which acted on behalf of the Presidency of Yugoslavia to resolve the situation by peaceful means. General Djukic confirmed that the leadership of Yugoslavia, or rather, the leadership of JNA reached on agreement with leadership of Croatia via authorities in Sibenik in order to evacuate these irregular rebel forces from that area in order to reduce tensions; that the Croatian side initially accepted that agreement, and then later on turned its back on it; and that the operation in Kijevo came about only when these members of Croatian armed formations, which as witness MM-79 said, were especially allergic to the JNA. So it was only then that the operation in Kijevo came about. General Djukic said that there were no wounded and no fatalities, that he was proud of that operation. And the Prosecutor is surprised by this or perhaps they regret the fact that there were no casualties. According to the evidence of General Djukic, the JNA at that time acted in the territory of its own country. It acted against rebel forces, not against the population. It had a goal to resolve this problem with as few casualties as possible. This was confirmed by the previously mentioned Prosecution witness and all Defence witnesses. Only the Prosecutor claims quite the opposite. Only the Prosecutor believes that there was this terrible plan to persecute civilians. Finally, Witness MM-79 - I do not wish to mention the post held by this witness - but this witness confirmed that during mass movement, known as Maspok in 1972, which was a movement in Croatian for secession of Croatia for declaring Croatia an independent state, he said that during Maspok, Tudjman, Mesic, Seks, and many other officials who were active in that movement were removed from political life. Witnesses confirmed that Mesic and Seks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say Maspok in 1972?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was Tudjman at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During these events, General Tudjman was a former general of the JNA, perhaps even an active general who was removed at that time. So in 1972 - there's a good reason why I'm mentioning this to you - the entire state, political leadership of Croatia, which carried out secession in 1991 had actually attempted to do this 20 years earlier and was removed from their offices at the time. Mesic was imprisoned as was Seks for their activities in 1972. We heard that from witnesses, including witness MM-79. Why is this fact important? It is important precisely because of paragraph 3 from the final brief of the Prosecution, where the Prosecutor said that they did not deal with 1972 in their indictment. Do you know why the Prosecutor mentioned this? They mentioned this because they wanted to conceal the fact that it was not in 1990 that the idea of Croatian independence arose as a result of a joint criminal enterprise or policies pursued by the JNA, Yugoslavia; but, rather, that this was an old political idea that was 20 years old and was prepared for 20 years and implemented in the most brutal way in 1990 and 1991. This is why I keep referring to this armed rebellion. This is why I believe this to be so important. Martic, as a crime inspector in Knin, and anybody else who came to testify here, Ministers of Foreign Affairs, Minister of the Interior, Ministers of Information, Prime Ministers, Deputy Prime Ministers, Commanders of police stations, Chiefs of police stations, so all of these people who emerged in Krajina in 1990 and 1991 were simply a reaction to evil, evil organised by Croatian authorities aimed at breaking up Yugoslavia violently. This was a reaction caused by fear; and according to the Prosecutor, this fear was unreal, unprovoked, and was generated by the stories spread by Mr. Martic and other Serbian leadership about the fact that there was no co-existence with Croats and that naturally all consequences were foreseeable, as was stated in the indictment. This is an absurd thesis. As to the nature of this armed rebellion, as to the nature of what transpired there in 1990 and 1991, this was something that the first witness for the Prosecution spoke about, witness Dzakula. But in order for us to understand the essence of these events, the tragedy of the situation, the tragedy of the Serb residents in Croatia, and the tragedy of Mr. Martic personally, who is an innocent man, who has been kept here for 1.704, four years and seven months, for their sake we need to say that this armed rebellion was the only joint criminal enterprise that existed in the territory of Yugoslavia, in 1990, 1991, and 1992; and that everything that happened until the end of 1995 was the implementation of that armed rebellion, the aim of which was to break up Yugoslavia, create independent Croatia, eliminate Serb population as population that was of different ethnic origin and different religion. They wanted to create a mono-ethnic state. That was their goal. As for the means used to achieve that goal, we will see that in a video excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is an excerpt, Exhibit 926, about JNA soldiers killed at Korana bridge in April of 1991. At that time, pursuant to the proposal of the European Commission, all decisions taken by Croatia were suspended and there was an alleged cease-fire. Please look at these people, the JNA soldiers. This will prompt you to come to the realisation that there were all Serbs, JNA soldiers. And you should wonder whether the people who watched this, observed this, had any reason to fear for themselves. One of the perpetrators, whose name is Hraston has not been convicted to this day for procedural reasons. He was acquitted. This will make you realise what the term "Ustasha" stands for, what kind of people they were. Witnesses told you about knives and other things they used. Exhibit 3 also speaks of that. In the Second World War, according to General Forcina [phoen], who was in Croatia, 715.000 people had their throats slashed, not killed, but throats slashed. And Ustashas used knives and sledge-hammers. You can will see what effect a sledge-hammer causes opposite a human head. You will see what Ustashas did when they came across people they wanted to get rid of. This is footage from 1951. You see a neck, please pay attention to the neck. This man had his throat cut. Witnesses confirm that these soldiers were captured, disarmed, forced to lie down, and then they massacred them. Witness Peric spoke of this, and this event was mentioned by many other people. I regret the morbid nature of this footage. I regret having to show this to you, but you need to see what Ustasha knives and sledge-hammers can produce. Witness Macura translated a book of an Italian author of Ustasha crimes, saying that he showed a cross, a gun, and a bomb; and then Ustasha leaders said that these symbols will be the symbols that we will fight with. This is something that was done between 1941 and 1945; and according to President Tudjman, this represents the tendencies, historical tendencies of a Croatian nation. And the Prosecutor believes that there was no reason for reason for Serbs to fear, that there was no hate speech, and that Serbs exaggerated this or amplified this. Look at these people, they are nothing but Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask a question, Mr. Milovancevic. I notice that several of those corpses are sutured in the chest here. Was that as a -- what was that as a result of? Was that as a result of an operation to determine the cause of death, or was that part of the killing? Are you saying that as they were being killed they were killed and then they were sutured? They were cut open and then they were sutured again? Who caused -- who sutured them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to testify about this. Let me just comment on this movie just to save some time. I can just tell you very briefly because I know the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I will not be testifying. Let me just tell you one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me control the proceedings. If you don't have evidence on record explaining to us how those suturings came about, then don't answer the question. I thought you were going to say to see witness so-and-so told us this is how the suturing came about. If you don't have that evidence, don't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not address this issue. I will not answer the question, in compliance with your order, but let me just say that this exhibit begins with footage showing the handover of the bodies. At the beginning of this clip, the bodies are offloaded from the trucks. So they are taken over. The Croatian side handed them over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. Please don't testify. You showed us the clip. We can see what the happening on the clip. Don't tell us what -- if you don't have a witness who told us where they were being offloaded from, don't testify. We saw that clip. It speaks for itself. You may carry on with your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The armed rebellion that we spoke about is important for this case, the case against Mr. Martic, because it was designed and organised. It was prepared for years by the same people. It all started in 1972. This is when this idea came about -- in fact, in 1971. You asked me if this was 1971 or 1972, the mass movement, the Maspok, the nationalist movement in Croatia designed to -- for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia. It actually happened in 1997 -- 1971 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- So you were right when you corrected me initially. The armed rebellion itself did not begin when the armed conflict broke out on a specific date. Prosecution witness, or rather, Defence witness General Djukic said that on the 23rd of March, 1991, the Croatian leadership declared the JNA to be an enemy force. Prosecution witness Dzakula, the first witness to appear in this case, gave evidence that in 1990 Croatia was a federal unit; and that in accordance with the Croatian constitution valid at the time, Croats and Serbs had the status of a nation. This witness also confirmed that the first elections in 1990 - I'm talking about witness Dzakula - Serbs in the entire territory of Croatia, with the exception of five municipalities, that they voted for the communist league of Croatia, the party of democratic changes, led by Mr. Racan. This Prosecution witness also confirmed that in the pre-election campaign the HDZ started displaying the new flag with the chequer-board symbol, that Ustasha slogans were made, that statements were made to the effect that Croats were suppressed by Serbs, that the Serbs dominated the political sphere. And this is how the armed rebellion was being prepared. This is a comment that I am making now in my closing argument. This is how hatred was engendered among Croats, the hatred against Yugoslavia and Serbs. And as regards the alleged supremacy of Serbs over Croats in Yugoslavia, this witness said that Stjepan Mesic, a Croat, was the president of the Yugoslav Presidency. He was the president of the federal state. The Prime Minister was a Croat, Ante Markovic. The Minister of Foreign Affairs was again a Croat, Budimir Loncar. The Minister of Defence was half Croat, Veljko Kadijevic. This is what Prosecution witness Dzakula said. The Prosecutor referred to Kadijevic as a Serb; whereas, he was in fact a half Croat. That's what the Prosecutor did in his final brief. Antun Tus, the commander of the air force, was a Croat. He was one of the deserters that we spoke about earlier when we spoke of Imre Agotic. The head of the security service in Yugoslavia was Draga Mutic [phoen], again a Croat. Key posts in the Croatian navy were held by Croat admirals. In the JNA navy, General Spegelj had been the commander of the 5th Military District for years. In 1990, the commander of the 5th Military District was Konrad Kolsek, a Slovene. This military district was headed in Belgrade. The commander of the Belgrade army was Spirkovski, a Macedonian. Yet, despite all this -- yet, despite all this, in the pre-election campaign, statements were made that Croats were exploited in Yugoslavia. The armed rebellion led by the Croatian leadership was a crime against peace. This was an effort to break up a sovereign state, Yugoslavia, a state of peace turned into a state of war, causing great damage. The worst damage was suffered by the Serb population in Croatia, and this population was not the victim of one extremist speech, individual extremists in the HDZ or in the Croatian political leadership. The cause for their suffering and their ordeal was a widespread campaign to declare Serbs bandits, the factor that causes the disturbance, people who had to be eliminated. You heard Defence (redacted) (redacted) Zagreb because of threats that he would be killed. You heard witness MM-90, the Minister of Justice and Administration, a judge from Knin and Drnis who had to flee Drnis in 1990 because he was told to flee. We can no longer guarantee that you will live or keep your job. Your family can stay until the end of the school year. This was in May, so the school year ended in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise, but Mr. Milovancevic mentioned the name of one of his own protected witnesses. It's at line 16 of page 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, apparently the person you mentioned at line 16 of page 37 is a protected witness, and he is a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely gave the pseudonym, but I may have given some details that could lead to his identification. But these are personal details. I'm not opposed to the redaction, so I agree. Let us not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We shall then take out line 16 of page 37. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence witness Branko Popovic, who's been a lawyer in a bank. He's worked there for 25 years. You've seen him. He's a lawyer. He's a calm person. He was a founder of the SDS, together with Mr. Raskovic and Mr. Dobrijevic. He testified about the persecution campaign. The Prosecution said, Where does it say in a declaration signed by 20.000 people from Sibenik, where does it say persecution; yet this was a document made in the heart of Europe. This is a declaration that is signed. This is something that is covered by the Croatian press TV. Witness Licina said that this was discussed in the Croatian parliament. We showed exhibits to this effect. This declaration says, You are not wanted. It would be good for you to disappear. As a result, he had to leave his job. Jovan Raskovic had his employment terminated. Dobrojevic suffered the same fate. Yet, the consequence -- the consequences are much worse. I'm talking about the system. I'm talking about the intent. This is how the Croatian population was being indoctrinated, to be hostile towards this minority population in its territory. Serbs are evil they are Chetniks. All evil may be used against them. This is in fact what happened. All means were used and let's see how they were used. Prosecution witness Dzakula says, "The pre-election campaign run by the HDZ," so we're talking about May 1990, "could be qualified as nationalist in relation to Serbs." Serbs were particularly upset. They felt fear, and this engendered a response among the Serbs. But you see, Your Honours, the Prosecutor allegation that the criminal Serb leaders, the Knin leadership, the alleged criminal Mr. Martic, created this exaggerated fear among Serbs to get support for their ideas. Yet, the first witness to appear in this courtroom, the Prosecution witness, says that at the election, almost the entire population of Serb background voted for a party led by Ivica Racan, and this witness goes on to explain why it is so. And he says they expected this party, with the Croatian politician, Racan, at its head, to ensure a joint future, a joint life for Serbs and Croats in Croatia. This was the expectation that the Serbs had when they gave their vote to the SDP party. They expected this, yet they were betrayed. They wanted, they expected to live in their common state, Yugoslavia; that Croatia would not secede from Yugoslavia. This is what they expected Ivica Racan's party to advocate, to do. They expected that they would remain a constituent people in Croatia. They expected that the HDZ would not turn them into a national minority. They expected that they would be protected and that they would not be fired simply because of their ethnicity. And they were, in particular, concerned by the new symbols that were introduced in Croatia. This caused a particular concern and worry among them, and witness Dzakula goes on to explain that horrible crimes were committed in World War II under the same flag. In paragraph 3 of his final brief, the Prosecutor says, We're not talking about the period between 1941 and 1945. Do you know why he says that? Because failure to mention the terrible crimes that were committed against the Serbs in the independent state of Croatia by the Ustasha authorities is the only way in which the Prosecutor can build this fabrication about this unfounded, irrational fear on the part of the Serbs. I don't know what to use to illustrate this to the Prosecution. Imagine a situation in France, the Netherlands, Poland, England, if you had a government in 1990 that would suddenly declare our flag is the flag with the swastika that was used by Hitler. And everything is suddenly turned on its head because this is a flag that is the symbol of the crimes. Today you have a response, even if just a small Nazi flag appears somewhere. And now this is the situation that we had in Croatia. This is not -- the Serbs were not opposed to it because it had been an ancient symbol used by Croats. Witness Dzakula said, My grandparents were killed. They were put in concentration camps under this flag. Exhibit 3 confirms how many people were killed under that flag. And the Prosecutor says, Well, what's wrong with this flag? Well, let him try and re-establish Hitler's flag in his own country and then let us see what the response would be, both by the population and by the authorities. Parallel to this pre-election campaign that Prosecution witness Dzakula said was a nationalistic one, he went on to say that the HDZ proposed a new constitution where Serbs will become an ethnic minority. The living conditions deteriorate for Serbs in their everyday lives; in the schools, in the hospitals, in the administration. Serbs are being fired or they are forced to go into premature retirement because they're Serbs. So we're talking about 1990. Serbs were upset. Serbs were afraid, witness Dzakula said. And the Prosecutor acts as if he, himself, had not called this witness at all. Defence witnesses confirm all such statements made by this Prosecution witness. And the Prosecutor pretends that this was not so and he harps on his argument that this fear was unfounded, asking the witnesses such questions. But before asking our witnesses about this fear, let us see what Prosecution witness Dzakula says about this fear and the response on the part of the Serb population. This is what he says. In the pre-election campaign at the very beginning, in 1990, Tudjman spoke about the independent state of Croatia, the Second World War state, as an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people. The most powerful politician in Croatia, its president, publicly states - witness Dzakula says - that he is happy that his wife is neither a Jew or a Serb. And the Prosecutor then cynically asks, Did you ever hear any public threats of genocide? I cannot describe this in any way, apart from an announcement of evil, that evil would come about. The witness confirmed that he knew about General Spegelj and his plans for an armed rebellion, and he confirmed, page 485 and forward, that General Spegelj said - so I'm quoting Prosecution witness Dzakula - there's nothing more for the army here. And let me remind you, the army he is talking about is the JNA, the regular armed force. This is October 1990. I'm trying to trace the origins of the armed rebellion. It will be completely destroyed, Spegelj said, according to witness Dzakula. I designated five people per each officer. We will eliminate them physically. Somebody would knock on their door, the door opens. Witness Dzakula illustrates Spegelj words by saying, Bang, bang, bang. A pistol would be fired, then the man would walk down the stairs. The JNA officers were to be killed on their doorsteps. Not a single JNA officer will reach the barracks, Martin Spegelj, the Minister of Defence of Croatia, a former JNA general, stated in that year, and yet the Serbs are alleged to have been terrified without any cause. There was to be a war with no mercy for anyone, either for women or for children. Shells would be fired into homes. The problem of Knin would be resolved with a massacre. In October/November 1991, Croatian minister in the new independent state of Croatia under Tudjman's leadership was saying these things, according to Prosecution witness Dzakula. At that time Croatia was a federal unit of Yugoslavia, and the ZNG could not exist legally under the constitution. He goes on to explain that the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, was the embryo Croatian army, a formation established by Tudjman. So it is quite clear who was organising and leading an armed rebellion. The ZNG in early 1991 was founded at a time when only the JNA and the TO were permitted to exist as armed forces on the territory of Yugoslavia, which included Croatia. This witness also explained that after the elections and the victory of the HDZ and the inauguration of the new government in 1990, preparations were set in place for a new constitution to be adopted. More and more was said against Yugoslavia and against the Serbs. Serbs were dismissed from their jobs. Serb policemen were retired prematurely so that new Croat policemen could be employed, and then the Serbs responded by self-organising. They held a rally Serb. They tried to use political means. The rally demonstrated the declaration of the historical right of the Serbs to self-determination and to continue living in the Republic of Croatia on their national and ethnic territories. Together, with the Office of the Prosecutor, we agreed on the fact that the SAO Krajina was an autonomous area within Croatia in December 1990, when it was promulgated, and that Croatian laws were implemented on its territory; whereas, the Prosecutor says that Martic and others were preparing for the secession of Krajina from Croatia and its accession to Serbia. In this indictment, the Prosecutor claims there was a joint criminal enterprise with the aim of establishing a single state under Serb domination which will be cleansed of all non-Serbs through crimes. This is an argument that the Prosecutor gave up in the Milosevic case. The Prosecutor said, Gentlemen, we have joined three indictments because of your thesis on a Greater Serbia; and his direct response was, I never charged Mr. Milosevic with Greater Serbia. And what is the Prosecutor doing here? He is charging both Milosevic and Martic with the idea of a Greater Serbia; however, we will deal with this a little later. What I have said so far is only a small segment from the Prosecution evidence testifying to the atmosphere of fear that existed on the territory of Croatia. Witness Ljubica Vujanic testified that she attended a meeting with Mr. Babic, and she was shocked to hear the Serbs from Western Slavonia speaking about people going missing. Prosecution -- Defence witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Dobrijevic spoke about Serbs going missing and 611 people being killed in Sisak. Exhibits 1013 and 1014, introduced through witness Dobrijevic, showed that Amnesty International in 2003 spoke about a systematic persecution campaign in the area of Sisak in which people went missing, were killed, were abducted, or threatened, only because they were Serbs. The Serbs did not approve the independence of Croatia, and all the witnesses have stated this because they were afraid that the crimes committed in the independent state of Croatia would be repeated. The Prosecutor, however, says they had no reason to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) when asked by the Prosecutor who threatened to kill him, spoke about the campaign that was being waged in Croatia. The witness was asked who was saying there would be genocide, but the leader of the Croatian state was saying that the platform of his party was based on the ideas of Ante Starcevic, who he refers to as the father of the Croatian nation. Witness Dobrijevic claims that he has a list of 611 people, and he was upset that we did not tender this list to the Chamber. Kirudja, a Prosecution witness, testified that in meetings with the Croatian leadership, the Croatian Ministry of Defence, he was constantly being told to tell the Serbs that the long Croatian arm and Janko Bobetko would get them. When you look at all this, the Serbs organised in the Krajina area - and let's not go into detail again - was due to reasons explained in detail by Defence witnesses, by (redacted) witness, also by MM-90, by Dzakula who was a Prosecution witness. They all confirmed that this was a response to the autism of the Croatian authorities, who responded to requests to have cultural autonomy to state terrorism and who sent troops who disarmed regular police stations of the MUP of Croatian which were located in majority Serb areas. According to Exhibit 1.005, these confiscated weapons were distributed to the Croatian population in Obrovac, Benkovac, and Zadar. Exhibit 1.005 is a letter of protest written by 122 policemen from the Zadar SUP of both Croat and Serb ethnicity, because in October 1990 such things were happening. In a multi-ethnic milieu when you arm a single ethnicity, the majority population and organise a rebellion, the minority population can only feel fear and expect evil, as confirmed by witness MM-90. Everything that was done by the Serbs says witness (redacted), a Defence witness, was a logical response. He says we were ex-communicated. The Croatian population in Croatia was basically killed as far as their civil rights went. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything said by the Prosecutor in their final brief and closing arguments about the events in Pakrac, Plitvice, Borovo Selo happened contrary to what their witness Dzakula said. Witness Dzakula also explained that at Plitvice an armed incident broke out on the 31st of March, 1991, completely ignoring the fact by Mr. Dzakula that on the previous day, the leadership of SDS decided to have negotiations with the Croatian side. And the response to such a message of Serbs was an incursion on a religious holiday, when that is not expected, when that is a blasphemy. Witness Dzakula says, I took part in negotiations. At that time the future president of RSK, Hadzic, was arrested and badly beaten. Witness Dzakula says I took part in negotiations to have the Serb roadblocks from Borovo Selo removed. In negotiations with Croatian authorities, this is when it was done, and Serbs agreed to that. Witness confirmed that on the 5th of May, 1991, Tudjman appealed to the population to rebel against the JNA; and that on the following day, following mass demonstrations, a JNA soldier was strangled. Witness said that he heard of mass disappearance of Serbs from Sisak; that in October of 1991 in Pakrac, Korana, and Marino Selo - and this is something the Prosecution has known for a long time - camps were established to liquidate Serbs. He confirmed allegations and the report that in municipalities Daruvar, Podravska, Slavina, Grubishino Polje, Pakrac, Okucani from October to December 1991, 4.118 Serb houses were destroyed, 27 churches. He confirms that in 1991 in the territory of Croatia, over 80 Serb churches were destroyed. He confirms the document of the crisis in Slavonska Pozega ordering the Serb population to leave their villages, to take money and valuables and leave. He confirms, saying that those who had left and didn't fall into Croatian hands were alive, and the villages were burned down together with anyone remaining there. He says that on pages 537 and 538 of the transcript. Do you hear what the Prosecution witness says, Your Honours? Terrible crimes, terrible crimes against international humanitarian law were committed in the territory of Yugoslavia in 1991, as evidenced by the Prosecution witness. Did the Prosecutor ever prosecute anyone for this? And they are duty-bound to do that on the basis of the charter establishing this Tribunal. Why are they saying that the Defence is using tu quoque thesis incorrectly? This Defence witness said that he signed Daruvar agreement with witness (redacted); that pursuant to this agreement there was to be a rationalization in lives, small steps aimed at re-establishing mutual confidence. Would you please redact this sentence. I mentioned a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret this. And in this particular case, Mr. Martic was accused of arresting Mr. Dzakula and the other person signing the agreement, I don't know his pseudonym right now, and that he did that only because they wanted to negotiate with Croatians, which is a blatant lie. Witness Barriot said that there was a general deficit of all supplies; medical supplies, pencils for school, electricity. There was nothing, nothing whatsoever. Why am I saying this in relation to the armed rebellion and what happened in 1991? I'm saying this because I want to show that the OTP claims that the population had irrational fear generated by the propaganda of hate and then responded to that. I want to show that such claims were denied by whole myriad of documents. The Prosecutor mentioned victims yesterday, Ante Marinovic and Jasna Denona who were victims of the tragic event in Bruska. I will ask if this is normal and logical for the person who comes to kill somebody to give his name and affiliation. If indeed a policeman was a murderer, then the police would find such a person, and that is not the case, Your Honours. This bandit, this monster, who had come to kill ten people, just looked for the easiest way to have the door opened to him. It was dark. This was in Bruska. It was a distant, remote village, where people do not easily open their door at night. But if you tell anyone on earth, This is police, open the door, naturally they will open the door. I'm reminding you of this tragic event because this is a good illustration of how the Prosecution construct their indictment. It is indisputable that these people were victims. utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have indirect evidence, Your Honours, and that's what I was about to speak of. And this is the circumstantial, indirect evidence that speaks of the attitude the Serbs had towards Croats, and that leads us to a conclusion that the story about the policeman as a perpetrator is completely uncorroborated by any serious piece of evidence. There is none, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I am stretching my imagination as far as I possibly can. I am trying to find out how the hospitality of Serbian people is an indirect confirmation that the person who attacked was masquerading as a policeman. But anyway, that's your submission. Carry on.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. What I wanted to say was Jasna Denona and Ante Marinovic, as victims and Prosecution witnesses, directly deny the claim of the Prosecution that Martic and his entourage that stands accused with him generated among Serbs a fear of Croats, and that then he transformed this fear into hatred of Croats and intolerance. The Serbs kept Jasna Denona in their village for a year in a completely armed village and she was save there. The Prosecutor does an incredible thing there. He mentions an incident in the Knin hospital when somebody comes in an uniform, and we should believe Ante Marinovic, the victim. Why should he invent this? So somebody comes and says, This Ustasha should be killed. And this is enough for the Prosecutor to make inferences on the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. At the same time, they failed to mention to you, Your Honours, what the same witness said, that a Serb doctor who saved this victim's life kicked out this scoundrel from the hospital. This is the attitude of the medical staff in this particular case, for which credit should be given to Mr. Martic as a member of the government cabinet, because this illustrates the attitude of the population towards Croats and those who threatened them. Prosecution witness Dzakula confirmed the events in the Medak pocket and the statement made by General Jean Cot, the scorched earth policy.
