A Defence witness says this and perhaps he should not be trusted, but this is Kort Bolevik [phoen] speaking. And witness Kirudja said that at that time Croatia wanted to deny hospitality to UNPROFOR and to undermine the cease-fire agreement that was prepared and signed on the Invincible, the destroyer; yet the Croatian side kept accusing the Serb side of wanting to undermine the agreements and wanting to actually engage in war. 30.000 armed Serbs wanted to inflict a military defeat on the heavily armed Croatian army that had 200.000 people under arms and six brigades at that time, in 1991. utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Just to remind you, Mr. Milovancevic, you've got to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be hard to do, because I think that it would be very difficult for the Defence to be cut off in its closing argument. You asked me for my estimate. I tried to be honest. It would have been easy for me to tell you, Yes, I would be done today. But I didn't want to do that because I wanted to be honest. I will take measures to focus on those elements that are relevant for the Defence, and I will try to be as efficient as possible. Thank you. I would like to correct an error that I made at -- in the course of my closing argument. I referred to a witness who signed the Daruvar agreement together with Mr. Dzakula, and I did not know his pseudonym. This is MM-105. I mentioned MM-115 and 75. I was mistaken on both those when I did that. So the witness who signed the Daruvar agreement together with Mr. Dzakula was witness MM-105. You see, Your Honours, why did the Defence take so much time to point to certain facts that we all heard here, the evidence that was led in this courtroom? Simply to show to what extent the claims made by the Prosecution about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise are, in fact, contrary to the actual state of affairs. This is, in fact, a distorted picture, a distorted approach that is taken out of its context at the time and everything else. The joint criminal enterprise, as presented by the Prosecution and as charged by the Prosecution, is nothing but a construct. Now I want to speak about something else. What are the key pieces of evidence for the existence of JCE? The first one is definitely the testimony provided by witness Babic. In the course of the cross-examination, this witness committed suicide. In this case a decision was made not to suppress his evidence, although this -- such a decision has never been made. This has not been practiced in the civilised world. A witness committed suicide during his cross-examination. Mr. Babic, by the very fact of his suicide, demonstrated that he had been disturbed, mentally disturbed. He could not have been a witness before this Tribunal as such. The Parker Commission noted that Mr. Babic had covered his face during his testimony, that he had exhibited signs of nervousness. The security also noted that he would drink water often and he was nervous, that he exhibited signs of anxiety, that he felt that he was being exploited. And I wanted to point to one fact. Not suppressing the evidence of a witness that testified while he was mentally disturbed leaves open the possibility that such a witness remains a key witness against the accused. This has been highly prejudicial to the Defence, and Article 21 of the Statute has been violated; that's the article that states that both the Defence and the Prosecution are entitled to question all witnesses under the same circumstances. And this prejudice cannot be remedied in any way. Mr. Babic had to be questioned about the circumstances that may have confirmed or denied his way of reasoning, his confession, all the circumstances that surrounded those events. Now, in order to understand the Defence approach to the issue of the status that should be accorded to Mr. Babic's evidence, we should consider the following key facts. Radislav Maksic, a Prosecution witness, said about Mr. Babic the following, that he had the power as the Prime Minister over the Ministry of the Interior and that Martic was responsible to Babic, that Babic and Martic did not communicate at all. That's page 1175 of the transcript. Witness Maksic said that he had never seen them together, that the two of them could not see eye to eye on any issue. The impression that Prosecution witness Maksic got was that this was Babic's -- that Babic was to blame for this. This is what witness Maksic said at page 1176 of the transcript. Babic was an narcissistic person and was unable to accept anyone's opinion apart from his own. As for Exhibit 132, Babic's decision to remove from office General Djujic the commander of the Territorial Defence in Krajina in which Babic states that he is removing him on Djujic's own request because of Djujic's age and health problems, witness Maksic said, testifying under oath, that Babic is lying. General Djujic never submitted such a request. The real reason behind this is the disagreement between Babic and Djujic. Exhibit 128. Maksic says here that Babic's decision, as the Prime Minister of Krajina government, on the appointment of this witness Maksic, the commander of the TO, was made when Babic did not actually have the power to do so. According to this witness, Babic did as he pleased, and the witness went on to explain that he informed his command, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and that he was recalled back to Belgrade. Ljubica Vujic is the next witness, Defence witness, who testified about Babic. She had been a lawyer for a long time and she was the head of the commission -- the electoral commission. She said after the conflict in Plitvice, Babic made a decision through the Executive Council about the annexation of Krajina to Serbia, that Babic himself did that through Executive Council. She went on to say that Babic actually drafted the text on the -- on the referendum paper, and she actually participated in this. She went on to say that Milosevic was very angry. He was opposed to the annexation. The only issue for him was the survival of Yugoslavia. Ljubica Babic [as interpreted] explained that, swayed by Milosevic's anger, Babic amended the referendum question in such a way that his text, Are you in favour of the annexation with Serbia. He added the text, And the -- to remain in Yugoslavia. And this witness confirmed that Babic did as he pleased and that he went against Milosevic's wishes. This is Exhibit 144. This is the decision on the referendum question. Defence witness Ljubica Vujanic testified that as a member of the commission empowered by the Republic of Serbian Krajina Assembly. She -- she then made this referendum question, this decision. She took this -- she took this decision with her to Belgrade, that Milosevic and the Assembly did not want to even receive them and to accept this decision; and yet the Prosecution claims that this was done, that Milosevic and Babic did this in concert. And they did something -- one thing in public and one thing in private. Witness Lazar Macura, who is a teacher of English and Italian, a translator, says that Babic, as the president of the municipality, declared a state of war, which he could not have done. Only the head of state can declare a state of war. A president of the municipality can only declare a state of emergency. As regards the decision on the referendum in April 1991, witness Macura confirms what Ljubica Vujic said that Milosevic was opposed to Babic's view, that the referendum question should pertain to the annexation to Serbia, and that the only thing that Milosevic was in favour of was the question about remaining in Yugoslavia. Witness Macura explicitly says that Milosevic did not want to hear about any annexation with Serbia, yet Babic held his own. And in the end, witness Macura says that when Babic formed the Republic of Serbian Krajina government on the 29th of May, 1991, Milosevic was again opposed to this. He was in favour of lower-level institution, not the government; yet again Babic held his own. Witness Macura confirmed that Milosevic was in favour of Vance's Plan and Babic was opposed to it, that was the witness, and open conflict resulted. Witness Macura says that Yugoslavia and Milosevic accepted the Vance Plan because it did not want to become a victim of the conflict in Krajina, that Yugoslavia -- it was quite clear to Yugoslavia that Krajina should, once again, be part of Croatia, although this was not spelled out in the Vance Plan. Witness Macura confirmed that when talks were held about whether to accept the Vance Plan or not, at the Yugoslav Presidency in Belgrade, that's late January 1992, General Agic, the Chief of General Staff wanted to strangle a member of the Krajina delegation, telling him, You, Krajina riffraff. You want us to wage war against the whole world. These are very harsh words that show the attitude of the top officers in the JNA towards the Krajina leadership and the goals that the Krajina leadership wanted to achieve, yet all this means nothing for the Prosecutor. According to him, the presence of General Agic in Glina when the Assembly rejected the -- accepted the Vance Plan shows that this was a joint criminal enterprise, because Milosevic and the Krajina leadership do the same thing. They accept the Vance Plan. There is a serious conflict with logic here. Witness Macura testified that the Yugoslav leadership, when it discussed the acceptance of the Vance Plan, that they were in favour of doing so because they had to accept it, because the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Vladislav Jovanovic, the Yugoslav Foreign Minister, said that they threatened that Belgrade would be bombed if we did not accept. And the Yugoslav leadership did everything in its power to accept this plan. The Prosecutor uses Babic to prove that Milosevic and Babic were acting in collusion as part of the joint criminal enterprise, which is completely in contravention to all these facts. MM-78, a protected Prosecution witness, says about Mr. Babic, yet another Prosecution witness, Babic's political ambitions bordered on sick. But when he spoke about Mr. Martic, he said in Martic's behaviour, they went to school together. He did not discern any signs of jingoism or chauvinism or intolerance to Croats; and then in response to Prosecutor's questions, he says that Martic cleansed Vrpolje, Potkonj, Kijevo, that was all part of the plan. We will see why this witness said all those things, but apparently he let slip a sentence that was in fact true when he spoke about attitudes -- Martic's attitudes towards Croats. And we heard what his attitude was of Babic. His political ambitions bordered on sick. Milo Dradovesic, a Defence witness, confirmed that Babic, as the president of the municipality, declared a state of war; and that he called for a mobilisation of the Territorial Defence on the very same day, despite the fact that he was not in power to do so. This is something only the Yugoslav Presidency could do. We're talking of August 1990. This man wanted to be in command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There's a question that I wish to ask you. Who constituted the Yugoslav leadership at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you take into account the situation in January 1992 when talks were held about the deployment of UN troops in those areas, the collective Presidency of Yugoslavia existed at the time, but representatives of Croatia left it at that time. Because of the secession, we know that Stjepan Mesic, the Croatian representative said, I have done my job. Croatia is no more. The Slovenian representative also left because they had seceded. The Macedonian representative also seceded because they also decided to secede. And the BH representative was already there -- was still there, even though there were problems in that republic. Even though it was a Rump Presidency, it still had the authority to ensure law and order in the overall territory of the republic for as long as it functioned and existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You have got there by process of elimination, so who is there left now at this stage for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not Croatia is no more, but Yugoslavia is no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency of Yugoslavia was the collective head of state. It was composed of representatives of all the heads of state, and the representatives of two provinces that were part of Serbia. Serbia, as the federal unit, was the only federal unit to have two provinces. And these provinces also sent their representatives to the Presidency. An ethnic Albanian representative of Kosovo was, in fact, the president of the Presidency. So you had representatives of Serbia, Montenegro, Vojvodina, Kosovo, and I'm not sure whether the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina was also on board. But I think it was so because Bosnia and Herzegovina was in favour of the acceptance of the Vance Plan and the arrival of UN troops. So this was the collective head of state, the leadership of Yugoslavia, at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As witness Milan Dragisic said, not only did Babic illegally declare a state of war, but after the first multi-party elections in April and May 1990, Babic as the elected president of Knin municipality. With respect to the existing municipal organ, which has a long name, he renamed it the Council of National Popular Resistance, and he was its president. Babic denied this. Witness Dakic said about Babic that after the 16th of March, 1991, all power was in his hands. He also testified that Martic, as a minister of the MUP, was not more powerful than Babic; that this was impossible; that Martic was only a civil servant in the Krajina government, far, far below Babic in power and authority. And we were able to see this in the Prosecution evidence when the subsequent representative or president of the Krajina replaced a minister. This is elementary in the democratic world. Witness Dakic explained that Babic was the leading figure in the government and that he could do whatever he wanted. A lot of this was to the detriment of the Serb people. He also stated that both of them were popular. Martic was also popular but that was because he was brave, because he was a hero of the Serbian people. Martic's popularity was not that of a politician, it was that of a hero. When he spoke about the kinds of decisions Babic made to the detriment of the Serb people, witness Mile Dakic explained that after the incursion of Croatian policemen in Plitvice on to Serb ethnic territory, Babic personally on the 1st of April, 1991, issued the fatal decision to accede to the SAO -- to annex the SAO Krajina to Serbia. Babic insisted on a referendum on the annexation of the Krajina to Serbia. Unlike him, the Serb National Council was against the referendum on annexation and desired a solution within Croatia. This meant nothing to Babic, this witness explained. Because when he failed to gain the support of the Serb National Council, he used the Executive Council of the Krajina to implement what he wanted. We heard that Milosevic opposed this vehemently. As for Milosevic's attitude towards Babic's decision, witness Dakic says this referendum on the annexation of the Krajina to Serbia caused great damage to the Krajina. Milosevic did not support the referendum. As from that time, there was strained relations between Babic and Milosevic. This was testified to by a man from the inner circles of leadership in the Serb Krajina under oath. This witness also said that three days later Babic, as the president of the Knin Municipal Assembly, dismissed Lazar Macura as commander of the municipal Crisis Staff. Witness Macura, whom we mentioned just a while ago, mentioned that he was the vice-president of the municipality. And when Babic wrongly declared a state of war, the Crisis Staff should have been activated. Witness Macura explained that after declaring a state of war, Babic fled. He fled into the mountains and hid. He was not a hero, as Martic was. Witness Macura, as the vice-president of the municipality, then took over leadership of the municipal Crisis Staff, which was duty-bound under the existing legislation to take over in such situations. And for two days he was in charge of the barricades to ensure normal life in the area. Babic testified to the very opposite of all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. Milovancevic, really want to reveal the identity of MM-90? You're telling us what positions he held, what -- I don't want to repeat that. You see it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please have page 68, line 5 to 12 redacted. And, Mr. Milovancevic, in the interests of economy with time, I would suggest that you consider not just dealing with every little witness as what he said, but deal with the issues at stake, the counts, and get done with the job quicker. That way you'll finish today because the Bench is not inclined to give you tomorrow to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mentioned the posts held by this witness to show that he was very close to Mr. Babic. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Just go ahead. The problem is you're now identifying him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you want us to redact that what you've just said. You've told us he's close to Babic. Carry on. We've seen what -- you've explained it. We will redact it. We will see that he was close. What's wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please redact page 69, line 2 to 7. Carry on, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness I referred to was amazed by Babic's guilty plea, because it ran counter to everything that happened on the ground. Either he was under the influence of drugs or he had gone mad or there is a third explanation. The question arises as to why and how Mr. Babic made that statement. In The Parker Commission report, it says that after he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment - it was on the 29th of June, 2004 - Babic was distraught and announced his suicide. He said that to his counsel, and he repeated that subsequently. More than once he told the administration of the Detention Unit that he was being threatened by other prisoners, but a check revealed that this was not correct; then he felt threatened by the neuropsychiatrist in the Detention Unit, Dr. Vera Petrovic. Evidently, there was something wrong with this man's health. His Defence counsel testified that he lost 15 kilogrammes in a very small space of time. So this witness's credibility and ability to testify is in question. He felt used by the Prosecution when he was brought to testify in the Martic case. That's what his son said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have any medical evidence to tell us what caused what you claim to have been either his madness or confusion or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the report of The Parker Commission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which recorded statements made by Babic to counsel that he was going to commit suicide. It is a fact that on two occasions he mentioned that he would kill himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. The Parker Commission is not medical evidence. If that is the only evidence you are referring to, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I do have another question. To what do you refer when saying that Babic said to the -- told the administration of the Detention Unit that he was being threatened by other prisoners, but a check revealed that this was not correct? What check do you mean? What do you mean by "revealed?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on pages 6 and 7 of The Parker Commission report, it is stated that on the 30th of August, 2004, Babic's Defence counsel raised the issue of his security because Babic had said that he was being threatened and attacked in the Detention Unit, whereas on pages 6 and 7, The Parker Commission states that Mr. McFadden carried out an investigation and there was no confirmation that Babic had been threatened, that the medical staff observed that Babic was very nervous after being found guilty. On page 7 it says that counsel Miller said on the 30th of September, 2004, that Babic had lost a lot of weight very suddenly, that he was concerned about the intentions of the psychiatrist in the UN Detention Unit, Dr. Vera Petrovic, that he was concerned for his safety. He mentioned that again on the 17th of December, 2004 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What you answered to me was slightly different from what you said before, that a check had revealed that the threats -- the alleged -- the allegations of the threats by other prisoners were not correct. Now you said it was not confirmed. I wanted to clarify that. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may have spoken imprecisely, I apologise. I just wanted to point to the findings of the commission, which show that Babic was complaining of threats but that investigations show that these threats were nonexistent or unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, you are turning around what is in the report. The investigations didn't confirm it. They didn't show that allegations were incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On pages 7 and 8 of the Parker Commission report, it says that McFadden carried out an investigation and found no confirmation to corroborate Babic's statements that he was being threatened. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What Judge Hoepfel is saying to you is that to find no confirmation can be credited to saying that what is alleged is incorrect. You said a check revealed that what he alleged was incorrect; that's not the same thing as finding no confirmation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milovancevic .

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Parker's Commission found on the 22nd of February, 2006, a day before the relocation of Babic's family, Babic expressed extreme concern about these issues. Babic's concerns became more profound because of the problems experienced by his family in the course of their relocation while he was testifying. Why did I mention all these facts? We asked the Court to deliver to us a copy of the original statement, because every fact concerning Mr. Babic's health is very important to us in view of our standpoint regarding his health. What is important for the Defence is the following: As of August 2004, shortly after his sentencing following a guilty plea, the guilty plea was made while he was staying in a private house, a private home until his sentencing on the 1st of December, 2003. From the 1st of December, 2003 to the 29th of July, 2004, he was staying in a private home. A member of his family stated that he was visibly upset on his arrival here because he felt that the Prosecution was using him. The fact that Babic committed suicide indicates that he was distraught. A person does not put a nylon bag over their head and a belt around their neck if they are emotionally stable. It is, therefore, not clear to the Defence how it is possible that the defence of an unstable and distraught person, or rather, the testimony of an unstable and distraught person should be taken into account. If the Defence did not have access to this witness, which it did not, how could the witness have been upset and agitated? Who could have exerted pressure on him? Could it have something to do with the Prosecution? At a time when he was testifying in the Martic case, that was the time when the problems of his family were being dealt with. These are questions that the Defence wishes to raise, and yet the testimony of such a witness has been tendered into evidence and accepted by the Chamber. When it comes to the status of Babic and the joint criminal enterprise issue, there's something that needs to be said now. Joint criminal enterprise as an institution was introduced by the decisions of the Trial Chamber. It does not exist as such in the Statute and the Rules. When it comes to the criminal law and international criminal law, the general rule is that there is no extensive interpretation. Only what is stated in the rules is to be applied. Therefore, in our view joint criminal enterprise could not have been introduced into case law by decisions of Trial Chambers. This was something that only Security Council could have decided to introduce through their resolutions. The Statute envisages only two forms of criminal responsibility: Articles 7(1) and 7(3), which is individual and command responsibility. What is interesting is that this type of criminal responsibility was introduced in order to try, for example, Martic, where there were multiple perpetrators. However, it is unbelievable, Your Honours, that Mr. Babic was allowed to negotiate with the Prosecution while staying in a private house, which is completely contrary to the explicit rules of the Tribunal. He was supposed to stay, he had to stay, in a Detention Unit. He was tried separately from Mr. Martic, who simultaneously stayed in detention for four years, waiting for his trial to begin on the same facts. So Mr. Martic was denied the fact -- denied the opportunity to participate in the case against Mr. Babic for the same fact and to affect the course of that case; whereas, the Prosecution believes that that plea and the conclusions of that Trial Chamber need to be taken into account when rendering a judgement in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, based on your submissions at page 73, lines 15 to 25, are you saying that the Trial Chamber may not reach a finding in respect of joint criminal enterprise in this case because of the lack of authority, it not being appropriately done by the Security Council? Are you going as far as saying that, that the Trial Chamber is not entitled to make a finding for this reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is the possible of the Defence that this type of criminal responsibility is not envisaged by the Statute and that, as such, as a form of criminal responsibility it can be established only by the founder of this Tribunal, which is the Security Council. Therefore, the case law of this Tribunal indicating that this form of responsibility exists is not something that can be relied upon by this Trial Chamber. This Trial Chamber can decide on this form of criminal responsibility only upon receiving an approval, a consent from the Security Council. This is the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or they can amend the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you know of the doctrine of common purpose in ordinary common law at national jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence believes that this manner of introducing joint criminal enterprise as a form of criminal responsibility is a case of the Statute going beyond its competence, and the same is being done by Trial Chambers and the Prosecution. The Prosecution not only goes beyond the Statute, but they openly abuse this type of criminal responsibility to the detriment of the accused because they introduce a type of criminal responsibility which is to be applied when there are multiple accused, and then they try each of these multiple accused separately. For example, Mr. Krajisnik is, according to paragraph 6 of this indictment, a member of joint criminal enterprise. We had General Galic here. We had Mr. Seselj -- we have Mr. Seselj. We had Babic. Babic stayed in a private home while Martic perished in detention. They were tried separately. What was the purpose behind this, to abuse the procedure. In my eyes this is an open abuse of procedure, because the accused is denied a right by imputing to him a criminal responsibility that is not envisaged by the Statute, and then he is denied an opportunity to either deny his guilt or to lead evidence to disprove it. Now, whether this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just on that point. In many jurisdictions where there are joint trials based on joint criminal enterprise or joint purpose acting in concert, it is a fact that it's considered less prejudicial to the accused when the accused are tried separately than when they are tried together because there may be various interests to serve and prejudices and conflicting interests when tried together. So do you have anything to say in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps such practice exists; however, if a crime was perpetrated in complicity, when there were multiple perpetrators, then there is no reason to try them separately. It goes against the nature of the crime, and it is against the law. And in this particular case, it's a much more drastic example, the one that I spoke of earlier. One is allowed to enter into plea bargaining while sitting in a private home, and the other one is denied that right and is in detention. And when somebody hangs themselves and then their evidence is admitted, then in our eyes such evidence has no value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that another person was denied the opportunity of a plea bargain? One is allowed to enter into a plea bargaining while sitting in a private home while the other one is denied that right and is sitting in detention. Was Mr. Martic denied a plea bargaining? And who initiates plea bargaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't fully understand your question, but let me tell you what my position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want you to understand my question. Look at page 76, line 21. Okay. You say there: "One is allowed to enter into plea bargaining while sitting in a private home, and the other one is denied that right and is in detention." Now, sitting in -- now, I'm asking you. Has Mr. Martic been denied plea bargaining, and who initiates plea bargaining under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honours, and you put it with good reason. I wasn't referring to plea bargaining. I was referring to the right of the accused, Martic, to participate in this same trial as Babic. And when Babic, for example, reaches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just make sure it is clear and crystal. One -- where is that -- 21. You're saying: "One is allowed to enter into plea bargaining while sitting in a private home, and the other one is denied that right and is in detention." Sitting in a private home counts as detention, so what remains as plea bargaining. So the other one that is denied can only refer to plea bargaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying Mr. Martic was denied plea bargaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you retract that statement? You retract that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm giving an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I don't need an explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is important for me to explain why I said that and to give you the essence of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is it is necessary for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Babic is tried for the same acts at the same time while Martic is under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and is not allowed to affect the course of Babic's trial. If Martic were given an opportunity to participate in the trial, then he would have been able to say, You are not right to admit that into evidence; however, he wasn't allowed to use that in his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is something completely different from plea bargaining, and it's nothing to do with this trial here at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And I would like to add that the word "bargaining" sounds as if it would be some sort of deal between the parties, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not aware of that term in the system of this court. "Plea bargaining." This is a term used in some countries but not here. It is a plea agreement and not a bargain -- a bargaining. That I wanted to add, and I agree to the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept what you're saying, Your Honour, except that the word that I used meant that this plea agreement also incorporated the agreement between the sides, not only about the sentence but also about the fate of Babic's family. So through this agreement, they agreed on what Babic's family was to receive in return for his plea, guilty plea. As for the portion of your question that I failed to answer, Your Honours, who initiates such plea agreements. I guess it's the Prosecution. To use such a witness under these circumstances as a key witness, as the main piece of evidence to prove joint criminal enterprise goes gravely against all elementary basic principles which speak of equality of arms, at least that as a minimum. However, this was not the only thing that the Prosecution did during their case. Witness Babic is mentioned on almost every page of 160-page long brief as a key witness. The second witness MM-03 came to the courtroom having given previously a statement and having written that he wanted to go to a third country; that he gave inaccurate information to the immigration authorities; that he was rejected; that the lawyer handling that case told him, Why don't you go to speak to the Tribunal; and that he then went to speak to the Tribunal, or rather, not the Tribunal, the Prosecution; that he gave false information to the Prosecution in order for them to accept him testimony at all; that he attended 100 meetings with Mr. Martic; and that then the Prosecution accepted him as a witness, arranged for him to have residence in a third country, which would have been unavailable to him otherwise. He said that he had gone to that country with a fake passport. He stated that as a witness. And he explained that he agreed to testify because that was the deal he had with the Prosecution. They were to ensure his status and he would say in the evidence whatever was necessary; and then that man became the second-most important evidence of the Prosecution, confirming the existence of JCE. This witness plus Babic are mentioned on every page of 160-page-long final brief. MM-78, another witness, said that witness MM-03 has a tendency to steal. He stole several cars from a train. He stole from people. So this is a person who has a tendency to criminal activity, and he came here to testify as a key witness for the Prosecution. What is the Prosecution trying to achieve by such a selection of the witnesses? We will show this to you in the course of our final closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which you have only 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope what you mean is that I have only 15 minutes left today. This is the witness that spoke about the actions in Ljubovo. I'm sorry. This is the key witness of the crimes. He spoke about Ljubovo and Lovinac and of the attacks in those villages. And under oath, he testified that the aim of the attacks was to expel the Croatian population; and then he says as an aside, I heard on the radio that there were some soldiers there and some units there. Defence witness Ratko Licina testifies that near one of those villages there was a barracks; Cveti Rok, that was the largest weapons depot. This is a location near Lovinac, and this was the location that had to be deblocked because it was attacked and surrendered during the course of this action. And the Prosecutor is trying to suppress this evidence by offering this kind of testimony. In order to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecutor claims that the Territorial Defence was disarmed and one of the witnesses testified that the TO weapons were outside of the depots only in the areas where locations were very far away from the garrisons, and that the reason why the Territorial Defence weapons were collected was to misuse those weapons. And this was the intent of the newly appointed commanders that were appointed by the HDZ. The witness explained that the Territorial Defence is entitled to take the weapons out of the depots for the purpose of exercises, but then they had to put them back. And the Yugoslav Presidency had to intervene in order to prevent the bloodshed, but yet the Prosecutor uses this to prove that there was this huge conspiracy in place in targeting the unarmed civilians. All the crime base locations Skabrnja, Nadin, Saborsko where conflicts occurred, those were the places where Croatian paramilitaries were well fortified and deployed, well-armed, and measures were taken such as the last-resort measures. We spoke about Saborsko in great length in our final brief, so I will not go into that. And witnesses testified about this, a number of Prosecution and Defence witnesses: Nada Pupovac, Zoran Lakic. The Prosecutor uses this incredible way of dealing with things. Notes by Colonel Bogunovic, Exhibit 107, and then they say Colonel Dragovic, the police chief from Bankovac, is mentioned as being present at an operation on the 20th of November, 1991. And the Prosecutor explains, Well this is evidence that the police took part in this attack, as if he never heard what the commander of Territorial Defence and Defence witness Lakic said, that the Territorial Defence and its medical corps took part in this action and that the police only regulated traffic in that action. Because if you have artillery, seven; APCs; and three tanks going -- using the public roads, then this causes a problem. And if you have a reason to expect that there would be a conflict there, then you need the police to be in place. So the Prosecution is making those claims without corroborating them without any evidence whatsoever. The Prosecutor says that yet another piece of evidence of the existence of the JCE is the fact that the JNA expelled everyone, apart from Serbs; and yet our Defence witnesses say that 73 officers left, first Slovenes, Croats, Muslims, that the army was decimated, that its ranks were decimated. And Colonel Maksic Prosecution witness says that this was done at the behest of the secessionist leaderships because they instructed those officers to leave those ranks. A book by Zdravko Tomac, My View Behind The Closed Doors, speaks about that. He says this is the way we destroyed the JNA. And those who didn't want to join them, we told them even if you don't want to take part your families are jeopardised. This was a threat with physical elimination. Tomac said the JNA was destroyed from within in an organised rebellion, yet the Prosecutor accuses the Serbian side, the Yugoslav Presidency, of doing that in order to implement some kind of inferno plan by leaving only the Serb officers in place. The Prosecutor accuses the existence of the Vance Plan as evidence of joint criminal enterprise, bringing in witness Kirudja to testify, Charles Kirudja. And on page 747 -- in fact, Exhibit 747 from May 1992, it was confirmed by him, it is a UN report, and this is what this witness has in mind in this UNPROFOR report he says that General Spiro Nikovic ensured him that the JNA would leave behind it a clean administration in military and administration sense. So the JNA accepted the arrival of the troops, it undertook to pull out the JNA troops from the area, it did so within the time-limits that were prescribed, and this is confirmed by Security Council report from 1992, 24600, where it is stated that the JNA withdrew in good order. I have to apologise to the interpreters, I'm really going very fast. And this report states that the JNA, this is what Kirudja says, will leave the situation in Krajina or in UN protected areas, a clean and clear situation both in military and administrative terms, and JNA General Nicevic told the witness that there would be an agreement signed by Krajina and Yugoslavia as regards the status of the UN forces. To this respect, Mr. Kirudja said that the protocol between the UN and Yugoslavia will be binding on Krajina. So the JNA, as the federal army, deals with military and administrative issues, and everything that it does is binding on the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And this UN document states that Yugoslavia guaranteed that the Republic of Serbian Krajina would comply with all its international obligations. So when on the 28th of March, 1992, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 28th of April, 1992, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]-- set up the police units, the special police units, eight brigades, to act as the border police. We have a UN document to prove that Yugoslavia did this in accordance with its powers in its own territory, and that Krajina was obliged to comply with it. And Defence witness Djukic confirmed that he was appointed the commander of special police units. So the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, now we're talking about Exhibit 798, the decision on the establishment of those special police units, the administration for those units is established, and this is subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior, eight brigades will be established. This is a decision of the federal authorities, and it is pursuant to the decision of those federal authorities that the UN was actually displayed there. Djukic, Defence witness Djukic, said that this was implemented and so was Defence witness (redacted). Witness MM-96 says that this was, in fact, implemented. So all these people who were police chiefs in Benkovac, the Knin Interior Ministry Secretary, the Minister of the Interior in Krajina, Djukic who was the commander of the special units, they all confirmed that there was full cooperation with UNPROFOR. They all confirmed that UNPROFOR accepted those special police units. General Djukic also testified that when any problems occurred, when all of a sudden and despite all those statements that reports were being made to the Security Council to the fact that those special police units were, in fact, violating the Vance Plan then the agreed with the UNPROFOR to disband those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On his feet, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, counsel. The name that is mentioned at page 84, line 25, the second word of that name is a protected witness of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This name has been bandied amongst by yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague is right. Thank you very much for your warning. There are so many names and at times one simply makes a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the sentence at page 84, line 25 containing that name please be redacted. Our concern is that you were talking amongst yourselves there mentioning the name whispering with your mike open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Can you give me one minute to ask a question just before we knock off. Carry on. Just before we knock off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence witness Djukic, General Djukic, who was the commander of the special police units says that when it was determined that the job that the special police units were doing instead of UNPROFOR, in other words, acting as the border police instead of UNPROFOR on the demarcation line with Croatia, when this became an issue, the Krajina leadership agreed with the UNPROFOR command and those units were disbanded. Mr. Kirudja testified to that, and we have another document confirming this. That is Exhibit 760, an agreement between Mr. Martic and Mr. Morillon. That's a document dated 26th of September, 1992, and it's an UNPROFOR document. In paragraph 2 of this exhibit, it is stated first -- first of all, Mr. Kirudja speaks about a large number of reports on cease-fire violations on the Croatian side with the infiltration of Muslims. This is also mentioned in the report as 24600; and then in the next paragraph it says that the Krajina leadership, so paragraph 3 of Exhibit 760, it is stated that the Krajina leadership, that the Krajina police responds to those violations and incursions on the Croat and Muslim part by dispatching the special police units and Defence witnesses spoke about that. Witness Jarcevic said that there had been more than 700 attacks from the Croatian side to the Serb side in those protected areas. This is what Mr. Kirudja speaks about in this report. And Exhibit 760 states that Mr. Martic and Mr. Morillon achieved an agreement on the 15th of September, 1991, on the demobilisation of the special police units to be implemented in two stages. And General Djukic in fact did implement this agreement and Prosecution witness Kirudja confirms that. This agreement was implemented also through a decision taken by the Krajina authorities on the disbanding of the special police units. That's Exhibit 567 -- 576, dated the 28th of November, 1991. And here I have to stop in order to give you were you one minute for your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- and page 59 line 20 to 21 you had been talking about the question of expunging Mr. Babic's evidence from the record and that it was not done in this case, and then you said this has not been practiced in the civilised world. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I regret if this is what went into the transcript. What I was talking about is something different. I was talking about the case law applicable in the world today regulating the issue of admission of witness testimony of witnesses who died in the course of giving their testimony. And I wanted to point out the difference between those situations and the situation we had here with Mr. Babic committing suicide. Because if a witness dies of natural death, this is an incident that no party could have anything to do with; and then the Chamber weighs the extent to which this witness was questioned or cross-examined. But here I wanted to draw a distinction because we are dealing with a different kind of issue. We have a man who hanged himself. In my opinion, he exhibited all the signs of being emotionally deranged and the decision to admit evidence by such a man does not exist in the civilised world. What I meant by that is the case law in the most advanced countries. This is the sense in which I use this term. I don't know whether I was specific enough or not. I regret if this caused any misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That didn't cause any misunderstanding now that you have repeated it by implication this Tribunal is uncivilised by rendering the decision it rendered on the admissibility of that evidence. Is that what you are implying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Actually, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no way, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This can actually be interpreted in the beginning can be drawn from what you say. The civilised world doesn't do what you do; therefore, you are uncivilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I wanted to say is that such a decision by a Trial Chamber could constitute a precedent in the negative sense in relation to the case law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you indicating in the uncivilised sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I now regret having used this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- I should have perhaps used the term modern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let us state, Mr. Milovancevic, that we issued a very thorough decision and that you, Mr. Milovancevic, appealed against this decision and that the Appeals Chamber confirmed the decision and that we did not find relevant for the admissibility of the statement if this was a suicide or not. Can we leave it like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not leaving it. I'm still pursuing it. That has nothing to do with what I'm asking. What I'm asking is what you're saying today. The positive side is to behave in a civilised manner. We didn't behave in a positive side, in a positive way, in a negative way; therefore, we are uncivilised, not only us but also the Appeals Chamber because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is absolutely unacceptable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is absolutely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is inconceivable given my line of thoughts with the culture that I come from. It is completely unacceptable with decent manners. And with the attitude I have displayed toward this Trial Chamber during the past ten months, I hope that it was obvious enough that I treated this Chamber decently. I used this unfortunate expression, meaning the modern practice, modern law systems, and I ended up using this ugly term which I now retract with all apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem with you, Mr. Milovancevic, is that in the process of saying it was an unfortunate term, you go ahead and use it again. You have been just using it here now just before you referred to negative sense and positive sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a favour to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Namely, that this term, together with all my apologies be expunged from the transcript, because it absolutely does not correspond with what I wanted to say and with what I was going to say. You know, some terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- have a different meaning in Serb and in English. I'm not blaming the interpreters. I'm not saying that they translated this wrongly, but will you accept my sincerest apologies that this was the last thing on my mind. It is completely unacceptable and I apologise to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I accept your apology, Mr. Milovancevic. But if we expunge your apology from the trial record, then you haven't apologised. So we will only expunge the term that you used and not your apology. Is that okay? Because if your apology is expunged, then you haven't apologized. It's as good as being withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't mean to be ungenerous and I take Mr. Milovancevic at his word and nothing against him at all. I'm a little concerned about the precedent of expunging things that occur on the record. He's apologised. It's clear. We've resolved it. It's fine. I don't think there's any need to tamper with the record in this case. There's really no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Court adjourned until tomorrow in the morning. I beg your pardon, Judge Nosworthy has something to say. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We are adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
